books.section: Topic 4.2 The Rise of Political Parties and the Era of Jefferson, C. The Louisiana Purchase and Territorial Expansion

stimulus.source_note: The Louisiana Purchase treaty, 1803, in its embroidered presentation binding bearing the seal of the United States. U.S. National Archives, via Wikimedia Commons. Public domain.
stimulus.text: The Louisiana Purchase treaty, signed in Paris in 1803, shown in its embroidered presentation binding bearing the seal of the United States. By the treaty France sold the Louisiana Territory to the United States for $15 million.

source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, the Louisiana Purchase treaty binding (1803), public domain
stem: The Louisiana Purchase was an important factor in the development of American trade because it

options.text: opened new markets among the western Indian nations
options.misconception: Trade with western Indian nations was small beside the river trade; Jefferson wanted New Orleans and the Mississippi, not new Indian markets.

options.text: gave the United States New Orleans and both banks of the Mississippi River
added many French factories in the Louisiana Territory to the American economy
options.misconception: The territory held trading posts and farms, not many factories; its value was land and the river, not French industry.

options.text: made possible the immediate completion of a transcontinental railroad
options.misconception: The transcontinental railroad was not finished until 1869, more than sixty years after the purchase.

rationales.A: Trade with western Indian nations was small beside the river trade. Jefferson wanted New Orleans and the Mississippi, not new Indian markets.
rationales.B: The treaty in the image gave the United States the port of New Orleans and both banks of the Mississippi, the great highway for the farm produce of the interior. Background: American traders could now travel the river's whole length to the Gulf without asking a foreign power's leave, and trade along it boomed.
rationales.C: The territory held trading posts and farms, not many factories. Its value was land and the river, not French industry.
rationales.D: The transcontinental railroad was not finished until 1869, more than sixty years after the purchase.
rationales.general:
1. Look at the object. A treaty, sealed and bound, by which France sold Louisiana in 1803.
2. Ask what the buyer wanted most. New Orleans, the port at the mouth of the Mississippi.
3. Ask what control of the river meant. Interior farmers could ship their produce to the Gulf unimpeded.
4. Put it together. Land doubled, but the trade prize was the river and its port.
Remember: when land changes hands, ask which road or river the buyer really wanted.
